newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spaniards in day of mourning for slain politician.
newsitem.headline: Spaniards in day of mourning for slain politician.

text.p: Spaniards began a day of mourning on Monday for a young Basque politician kidnapped and brutally murdered by separatist guerrillas.

Mass demonstrations and work stoppages were planned throughout Spain in an unprecedented national outcry against the Basque guerrilla group ETA, which has waged a violent 29-year struggle for an independent homeland.

Miguel Angel Blanco, a 29-year-old town councillor and low-ranking member of Spain's ruling party, was to be buried on Monday, a day after he died in a coma after being shot twice in the head by his ETA captors.

With emotions running high, officials appealed for calm and police bolstered security around the offices of Herri Batasuna, the political arm of the ETA rebel movement, to prevent a repeat of attacks on Sunday by angry protesters.

The Pope denounced Blanco's killing as "an act of blood". French President Jacques Chirac called it "cowardly". Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro said it "offends the conscience of the whole civil world".
But the sense of outrage was greatest in Spain, where ETA's targeting of an innocent victim was interpreted as a sign of increasing desperation.

Blanco was the 10th person killed by ETA so far this year. The group had kidnapped 77 people in its history and set deadlines to execute hostages only twice before. In both cases, the threat was carried out.

Hundreds of thousands of people turned out in more than a dozen Spanish cities overnight to demonstrate against ETA, with the largest gatherings in Madrid and the Basque cities of Bilbao, Vitoria and San Sebastian.
"They are ... bravely taking to the streets and saying 'enough', but with a force, with an energy we have never seen," Basque Socialist leader Ramon Jauregui told reporters.
"We have known the inhuman cruelty of ETA, but we would never have believed they would sink to this level of degradation," Basque leaders said in a statement.
Blanco was found on Saturday bound and bloodied, two bullets lodged in his brain, two days after ETA guerrillas kidnapped him.

Rebels had threatened to kill him unless 500 ETA inmates were moved to prisons in the autonomous Basque region by 4 p.m. on Saturday. He died early on Sunday in a hospital in the Basque city of San Sebastian.
His casket was taken to a chapel in his hometown of Ermua, where thousands of mourners filed past late into the night.
Appearing atop a balcony at city hall, Blanco's family members clasped hands and wept while thousands of sympathisers chanted "ETA, enough. We want peace."
Overcome with grief, Blanco's mother collapsed in the arms of relatives.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and Crown Prince Felipe were to attend Blanco's funeral on Monday afternoon.
Blanco's killing unleashed a backlash against ETA.

In Pamplona, where Spain's famous bull-running festival was suspended for a day in solidarity with Blanco's family, dozens of protesters clashed with ETA supporters outside the offices of the group's political wing.
Police in riot gear sprayed teargas and swung batons to restore order. Eighteen people were injured.

ETA attacks have stirred a public outcry before. The group has killed 800 people in 29 years of separatist attacks. But it was the death sentence passed against such an outwardly ordinary person as Blanco that cut to the heart of Spanish society.
"Miguel could have been any one of us. That's why it hurts," said one protester in Bilbao.
Basque leaders asked for an hour-long work stoppage from noon on Monday in the Basque region of northern Spain to express "indignation" at the killing.
Spain's leading unions urged workers across Spain to stop at noon and observe 10 minutes of silence.

Basque leaders and a senior official of Aznar's centre-right Popular Party called for the isolation of Herri Batasuna, which holds seats in the Basque and Navarre regional parliaments and the national congress.
But in a statement issued on Sunday night, Herri Batasuna complained that the campaign against it was tantamount to political "lynching".
